items.title: Row Counts Won’t Save Your Cutover
items.author: FNU Aditya Ranjan
items.content:
A reconciliation-first approach to CDC into Redshift, and where GoldenGate and AWS DMS pipelines actually go wrong.

Cutover night. The row counts match to the last digit. Somebody posts a green checkmark in the channel and everyone goes to bed.

Three days later, finance asks why order totals for one region are off by a few thousand dollars. Nothing is down. Nothing alerted. The counts still match. That’s the problem.

The pattern is familiar to anyone who has moved a busy database onto a new platform. The pipeline gets built, the full load finishes, change data capture (CDC) hums along, and the team picks the one check that’s easy to run: count the rows. Counts catch missing data. They say nothing about data that arrived wrong, arrived twice, or never got its update.

This article is about the checks I’d automate before trusting either GoldenGate or AWS DMS to feed Redshift, and the lag arithmetic that tells you when the pipeline is falling behind.

  • Treat row counts as a smoke test, never as the exit criterion for a cutover.
  • Land every change as an append-only record, then apply the latest change per key. Don’t rely on Redshift to reject duplicates.
  • Alert on the slope of lag, and put source-side bulk jobs on a calendar.
  • Reconcile with bucketed checksums over the whole table, then drill into the buckets that disagree.

Every number below comes from one worked example with made-up data: an Oracle ORDERS table of 480 million rows being replicated into Redshift. It is illustrative, not from a real system, and I flag it each time.

1. Row counts are a smoke test

A matching count proves the pipeline didn’t lose or duplicate whole rows at one moment in time. It’s a useful first check, and I run it. But look at what it can’t see:

An update was lost or applied out of order

The row exists on both sides

A delete never reached the target

Counts drift, but only after enough deletes

A large text column was truncated in flight

Same keys, shorter values

An empty string became NULL (or the reverse)

Timestamps lost precision or shifted time zone

Same keys, different values

The same change was applied twice

Five of those six defects leave the count untouched or only occasionally move it. If your exit criterion is “counts match,” you’ve certified the easiest thing to get right.

People compare GoldenGate and DMS on feature lists. I compare them on what happens when something goes wrong, because that’s where the weekends go. This is my rule of thumb, not a law. Check licensing and the current documentation for your versions before you decide.

Extract reads the redo, writes trail files

A task on a replication instance reads the source logs

Trail files absorb the backlog (size the disk)

Source logs must stay available until the task catches up

Rich mapping and filtering

Table mappings and basic rules

You run and upgrade the processes

Managed service, fewer moving parts

High-volume Oracle estates, strict ordering, long-lived replication

Time-boxed migrations, small teams, AWS-native stacks

Whichever you choose, the target side looks the same, and that’s where most of this article lives.

3. Five stages, three checks

The pipeline is easy to draw. The discipline is in giving each stage a check that can fail loudly:

  • Is the backlog growing or shrinking? (Section 5.)
  • Does the number of changes landed per batch match what the source log says it emitted?
  • Does the content agree, not just the count? (Section 6.)

4. Land the changes, then apply the latest per key

I land every change as an append-only record with its operation, commit position and sequence. Then I apply only the latest change per key. Two reasons. First, retries and replays are harmless, because applying the same batch twice gives the same result. Second, Redshift doesn’t enforce primary keys. They’re informational, used by the planner, so the target will happily store duplicates and won’t tell you.

Untested sketch, Redshift SQL (check syntax against your cluster version; newer clusters also support MERGE):

CREATE TABLE orders_changes (
  batch_id BIGINT, op CHAR(1), commit_scn BIGINT, seq BIGINT,
  order_id BIGINT, status VARCHAR(20),
  amount_cents BIGINT, updated_at TIMESTAMP
);
 
CREATE TEMP TABLE latest AS
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT c.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY order_id
           ORDER BY commit_scn DESC, seq DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders_changes c
  WHERE batch_id = 1042
  ) AS t
WHERE rn = 1;
 
BEGIN;
DELETE FROM orders USING latest l
  WHERE orders.order_id = l.order_id;
INSERT INTO orders
  SELECT order_id, status, amount_cents, updated_at
  FROM latest WHERE op <> 'D';
COMMIT;

Deletes arrive as a change record, so the DELETE removes the old row and the INSERT skips it. Updates become delete-plus-insert, which suits a columnar store far better than row-by-row updates. In the worked example, 12 million changes a day split into 6.6 million inserts, 4.8 million updates and 0.6 million deletes (55%, 40% and 5%). Batching those is not optional.

5. Alert on the slope, not the level

Average lag is a comfortable lie. Here’s the arithmetic for the example. The table sees 12 million changes a day, about 139 a second on average and roughly 1,100 a second in the busiest hour (I assumed an 8x peak). Suppose the apply side can sustain 3,000 changes a second. That’s 2.7 times the peak. Healthy.

Now somebody runs a backfill that updates 40 million rows in an hour. That adds about 11,100 changes a second, for a total near 11,250 against capacity of 3,000. The surplus is 8,250 a second.

Using lag ≈ backlog ÷ apply rate as a rough estimate, a 5-minute target is breached after about 109 seconds, because the backlog passes 900,000 changes. By the end of the job the backlog is 29.7 million and lag peaks near 165 minutes. Draining it at the 2,861 a second of headroom takes another 173 minutes, so the pipeline is back to normal about 293 minutes after the job started.

A backfill that takes an hour at the source can cost you five hours of staleness downstream.

Two habits fix most of this. Alert when lag is rising for ten minutes, not when it crosses a line, so you hear about it early. And put source-side bulk jobs on a shared calendar, so the pipeline owner knows a surge is coming before the pager does. In DMS, watch the source and target latency metrics separately; they point to different bottlenecks (check the troubleshooting guide for your version).

6. Reconcile with checksums, not samples

The usual response to “counts aren’t enough” is to compare a random sample of rows. It feels rigorous. It isn’t, and the maths is short. If N is the table size, n the sample size and k the number of corrupted rows, the chance of catching at least one is about 1 − (1 − n/N)^k.

In the example, 480 million rows and 120 bad ones (0.000025% of the table). A 1-million-row sample finds at least one bad row 22% of the time. A 10-million-row sample finds one 92% of the time, and costs ten times as much. Checksums over the whole table find it every time, because every row is counted in some bucket.

So I bucket the keys, compute cheap aggregates per bucket on both sides, and diff the results. Here’s a query that runs unchanged on Oracle and Redshift (untested; adapt types to your schema):

SELECT MOD(order_id, 4096) AS bucket,
       COUNT(*) AS n,
       SUM(amount_cents) AS amt,
       SUM(CASE status WHEN 'NEW' THEN 1
                       WHEN 'PAID' THEN 2
                       WHEN 'SHIPPED' THEN 3
                       ELSE 0 END) AS st,
       MAX(updated_at) AS max_upd
FROM orders
WHERE updated_at <= :cutoff
GROUP BY MOD(order_id, 4096);

With 4,096 buckets, each holds about 117,000 rows. The 120 bad rows can touch at most 120 buckets, so the drill-down scans at most 14 million rows, 2.9% of the table. Two details matter more than the SQL:

  • Same cut-off on both sides. Compare the source as of a commit point and the target after it has applied everything up to that point. Otherwise in-flight changes show up as false mismatches and the team learns to ignore the report.
  • Hash functions differ between engines, so I compare counts, sums and maxima on normalised columns. For text columns, canonicalise first: trim, case, and above all the empty-string question (see the pitfalls).

7. A cutover runbook with gates

The template I’d steal: each step has an action and a gate, and the gate is a number somebody can check. “Three clean reconciliation nights in a row” beats “looks good.” The T+7 row matters too. Keep the reverse path warm for a week, because mismatches that survive three clean nights tend to be the slow ones: month-end jobs, rare code paths, the table nobody remembered.

8. Where I’d bet you’ll trip

  1. Empty string versus NULL. Oracle treats an empty string as NULL. Redshift doesn’t. Your counts match and your WHERE clauses disagree.
  2. Check how your tool treats LOB columns. Some modes cap the size and truncate silently, which is exactly the defect counts can’t see.
  3. If the source purges its logs before the pipeline reads them, you’re back to a full reload. Set the retention for the worst outage you can imagine, not the average week.
  4. Schema changes mid-stream. A column added on the source on Thursday breaks something on Friday. Freeze DDL before cutover and test one change in rehearsal.
  5. Precision, time zones and daylight-saving boundaries. Compare them explicitly; they rarely fail loudly.
  6. No owner for reconciliation. A report nobody reads is the same as no report. Give it a name, a schedule and a threshold that pages someone.

Counts are a smoke test. Land changes append-only and apply the latest per key. Watch the slope of lag and know your bulk jobs. Reconcile with bucketed checksums at a shared cut-off, and give every cutover step a gate that is a number.

items.title: Monthly Churn Times 12 Is Not Annual Churn
items.author: Malek Damiri
items.content:
A company reports 2.2% monthly churn. Someone multiplies by 12 and writes "about 26% annual churn" in the board deck. It looks like basic arithmetic. It's wrong twice, and the two errors don't cancel out.

The first error is the one people half remember from school: churn compounds. The second is bigger and less well known: the customers who churn in a typical month are not the customers you had at the start of the year. In a growing business, those two groups behave very differently.

Here's both, with a simulation and the SQL to get the real number.

If you lose 2% of customers in January, you lose 2% of a smaller base in February. Over 12 months, you keep 98% of 98% of 98%, twelve times. That's 0.98 to the 12th power, or 78.5%. Annual churn is 21.5%, not 24%.

"""Monthly churn to annual: multiplying by 12 vs compounding."""
print("monthly  x12     compounded")
for m in (0.01, 0.02, 0.03, 0.05, 0.08):
    print(f"{m:>6.0%}  {12 * m:>5.0%}  {1 - (1 - m) ** 12:>9.1%}")


def monthly_from_annual(a):
    return 1 - (1 - a) ** (1 / 12)


print(f"\n20% annual churn = {monthly_from_annual(0.20):.2%} a month, not {0.20 / 12:.2%}")

monthly  x12     compounded
    1%    12%      11.4%
    2%    24%      21.5%
    3%    36%      30.6%
    5%    60%      46.0%
    8%    96%      63.2%

20% annual churn = 1.84% a month, not 1.67%

At low churn, the difference is small. At 5% a month, multiplying says 60% and compounding says 46%. At 8% a month, multiplying says you lose nearly every customer in a year, which isn't what happens.

The same mistake runs in reverse. A contract business with 20% annual churn that divides by 12 to get a monthly figure for a lifetime value model will understate monthly churn and overstate lifetime value.

So: compound, don't multiply. But that's the small error.

Error two: the wrong customers

I simulated three years of a growing subscription business. The key assumption, which matches almost every real subscription business I've looked at, is that churn falls with tenure. New customers leave at 6% a month for their first three months, 2.5% a month until they reach a year, and 1% a month after that.

First, the usual monthly churn rate for 2025: customers who cancelled in a month, divided by customers active at the start of that month, averaged over the year.

-- monthly logo churn for 2025 (months 24 to 35): cancelled in the month / active at the start of the month
with months as (select range as m from range(24, 36)),
monthly as (
    select m,
           count(*) filter (where c.start_month < m and (c.end_month is null or c.end_month >= m)) as active_at_start,
           count(*) filter (where c.end_month = m and c.start_month < m) as cancelled
    from months
    cross join customers c
    group by m
)
select round(avg(cancelled / active_at_start), 4) as avg_monthly_churn,
       round(12 * avg(cancelled / active_at_start), 3) as times_12,
       round(1 - power(1 - avg(cancelled / active_at_start), 12), 3) as compounded
from monthly;

 avg_monthly_churn  times_12  compounded
            0.0221     0.266       0.236

2.2% a month. Times 12 is 26.6%. Compounded is 23.6%.

Now the question the board actually means: of the customers we had on January 1, how many had left by December 31?

-- what actually happened to the customers active on January 1, 2025
select count(*) as active_jan_1,
       count(*) filter (where end_month is not null) as gone_by_dec_31,
       round(count(*) filter (where end_month is not null) / count(*), 3) as annual_churn
from customers
where start_month < 24 and (end_month is null or end_month >= 24);

 active_jan_1  gone_by_dec_31  annual_churn
         3308             571         0.173

17.3%. The compounded monthly rate overstates it by six points. The multiplied rate overstates it by nine.

The reason is who's in the monthly numbers. Every month, the denominator includes customers who joined recently, and recent customers churn the most. In a growing business there are always lots of them. But the January 1 cohort doesn't get any new customers during the year. It only gets older, and older customers churn less.

Split the January 1 customers by how long they'd been customers:

-- the same, by tenure on January 1
select case when 24 - start_month <= 3 then 'a: 0-3 months'
            when 24 - start_month <= 12 then 'b: 4-12 months'
            else 'c: over a year' end as tenure_on_jan_1,
       count(*) as customers,
       round(count(*) filter (where end_month is not null) / count(*), 3) as annual_churn
from customers
where start_month < 24 and (end_month is null or end_month >= 24)
group by 1
order by 1;

tenure_on_jan_1  customers  annual_churn
  a: 0-3 months        676         0.257
 b: 4-12 months       1430         0.176
 c: over a year       1202         0.121

Customers who'd been around for more than a year lost only 12% over the next 12 months. Customers who were brand new lost 26%. The monthly churn rate is a blend of both, weighted toward new customers because a growing business keeps adding them.

They answer different questions, so each is right for something.

Monthly churn on the whole base tells you how much work customer success has this month and how much revenue you need to replace. It's an operational number. Use it to run the business month to month.

Annual churn of a starting cohort tells you how durable the customer base is. "Of the customers we had a year ago, 83% are still here" is what investors and boards are asking about. Use it for anything that sounds like a year.

tells you where the problem is. If new-customer churn is high and mature-customer churn is low, the problem is onboarding or fit, not the product. That's a very different fix.

What isn't right for anything is monthly churn times 12. It mixes a rate that's dominated by new customers with a time frame that implies the starting base. In a fast-growing business, it can overstate annual churn by half.

Everything here applies to revenue churn too, with one more complication: customers who expand often churn less, and larger customers often churn less than small ones. So revenue churn by month and revenue retention of a starting cohort can diverge even more than logo churn. Compute both from the same cohort query, swapping a count for a sum of recurring revenue.

One more trap. If customers sign annual contracts, they can only leave at renewal. A monthly churn rate on an annual-contract book measures which month the renewals happen to fall in, not how likely customers are to leave. For annual contracts, measure churn per renewal: of the contracts that came up for renewal, what share renewed. Then if you need an annual figure, that's already it.

Compound, don't multiply. Measure annual churn on a starting cohort, not by converting a monthly rate. And split by tenure, because the average hides the only thing you need to know: whether customers leave early or late.

items.title: Your AI Agent Has Permissions. Who Gave It the Authority?
items.author: Gaus Ahamad
items.content:
In late April 2026, a coding agent working for a small software company called PocketOS ran into a credential error in a staging environment. It didn't stop to ask anyone. It searched the project, found an API token in a file unrelated to its task, and used that token to delete a storage volume on Railway, the company's cloud host. The volume held the production database, and the backups sat on the same volume. The deletion took about nine seconds.

Founder Jer Crane wrote afterwards that the token had been created for routine domain operations through Railway's command line tool. Nobody at PocketOS knew it could also delete production volumes. The company restored from a backup that was three months old, then rebuilt the missing bookings from payment histories, calendar entries and customer emails.

Nothing in that story was a hack. The token was valid and the API call was well formed, so Railway did what the credential allowed. Every system in the chain was asked "can this caller do this?" and each one correctly answered yes. No system asked who had decided the agent should be doing it.

Security people keep two words for this. A permission is what a credential can technically do. Authority is the right to do it, and it has to come from someone entitled to give it. Most agents running today have plenty of the first and a thin paper trail for the second. This piece looks at how that happens and what a proper answer looks like.

Three questions that usually get asked as one

Authentication answers "who is this?" A password, a passkey or a signed certificate proves the caller is who it claims to be. It says nothing about what the caller should be allowed to do.

Authorisation answers "what may this caller do?" Roles, scopes and policies live here. A token that can read your calendar but can't delete events is an authorisation decision.

Delegation answers a question the first two skip: on whose behalf is this caller acting, and within what limits?

If you have ever sent someone to collect a passport or a bank document for you, you already know what good delegation looks like. You write an authority letter. It names you, names the person you are sending, says what they may collect, and carries a date. The clerk checks the bearer's ID against the letter. Your cousin walks out with one envelope, and he can't empty your account while he's there.

Software has mostly handled the same errand in two worse ways. Either the cousin gets your own ID card and the clerk believes he is you, or he gets a master key to the building. The first is impersonation. The second is a broad API key. In both cases the clerk has no letter to check.

RFC 8693, the OAuth token exchange standard from January 2020, draws this line formally. Under impersonation, the acting party is indistinguishable from the person it acts for. Under delegation, it keeps its own identity and acts as that person's agent. The word "agent" was in the RFC years before anyone attached a language model to it.

Why this matters more for agents than for scripts

A nightly cron job with an over-powered key was always a risk, but a predictable one. Its code did the same thing every run, and you could read that code.

An agent decides what to do at run time. Part of what shapes the decision is text it picks up along the way: a web page, an email, a GitHub issue, an error message. Auth0's identity team puts it this way: once behaviour is no longer fixed by code, the scope of the credential is one of the few controls you have left.

How agents usually get their access

The first time you connect an agent to a database or a cloud account, the quickest route is the credential you already have. That is usually your own, or an admin key sitting in a config file. Four patterns cover almost every setup.

A Cloud Security Alliance survey from January 2026 gives a rough idea of the spread. Of 228 IT and security professionals, 43% said their agents rely on shared service accounts and 31% let agents run under human user identities. 74% said agents often get more access than they need. 68% could not clearly tell agent activity from human activity in their own systems.

The sample is small and the study was funded by Aembit, which sells agent identity products, so treat the figures as a sketch. The shape is still familiar. PocketOS fits the first row of the table: a key made for one job that turned out to work for every job.

Standards people have noticed. An Internet-Draft on agent authentication, written by engineers from Okta, Ping Identity, AWS, OpenAI, Zscaler and Defakto Security, calls static API keys an antipattern for agents. Its reasoning is that they are long-lived bearer secrets, bound to nothing, and hard to rotate. The document is a draft and may change, but its authors include Brian Campbell, who edited RFC 8693.

The confused deputy, 38 years on

In 1988 Norm Hardy published a three-page note called The Confused Deputy. It described a compiler on a commercial timesharing system. The compiler had write access to its home directory so it could record usage statistics. The system's billing file lived in the same directory.

One day a user told the compiler to write its debugging output to a file with the billing file's name. The compiler obliged, and the billing records were overwritten. The user had no right to touch that file. The compiler did, and it couldn't tell whose authority it was using for that particular write.

An AI agent is Hardy's compiler with a much larger vocabulary. It carries credentials from whoever deployed it, and it takes direction from whatever text lands in its context window.

Researchers at Invariant Labs showed in 2025 that a malicious issue filed on a GitHub repository could hijack an agent connected through the official GitHub MCP server. The attacker needed no access to the victim's private repositories. The agent already had it.

Not every failure needs an attacker, though. In mid-2025, Replit's coding agent deleted a user's production database after being told not to change anything without permission. The PocketOS agent wasn't tricked either. On its own account afterwards, it guessed that the volume belonged to staging and never checked.

The same control stops both kinds. If the credential can't perform the damaging action, it doesn't matter whether the agent was fooled or just wrong.

What properly delegated access looks like

Very little of the fix is new. Most of it is OAuth plumbing that has existed for years and is now being pointed at agents. Six pieces do the work.

  1. The agent has its own identity. The IETF draft treats an agent as a workload with one unique identifier and short-lived credentials cryptographically bound to it. It also says the model itself must never see those credentials, so a prompt injection has nothing to leak.
  2. A person grants a narrow slice. The user signs in and approves a consent screen that names the agent and the specific access it wants. This is the authority letter being written.
  3. The token carries both names. After a token exchange, the access token lists the user as the subject and the agent as the actor.
  4. The token works in one place only. The MCP authorisation rules require clients to say which server a token is for, and require servers to reject any token that wasn't issued to them. Forwarding a client's token to another API is forbidden outright.
  5. Tokens are short-lived and fetched per task. The agent never holds a long-lived refresh token. A broker holds it and hands out a fresh, narrow token for each operation. Revoke the connection at the identity provider and no new tokens are issued.
  6. Scopes start small. MCP's security guidance recommends a minimal read-only baseline, with extra scopes requested only when a privileged action is first attempted. It warns against wildcard scopes and against bundling unrelated privileges to avoid future prompts.

Here is what step 3 looks like in practice. This is the payload of a delegated token for an invented scheduling agent:

{
  "sub": "meera@example.com",
  "aud": "https://calendar.example.com",
  "scope": "calendar.events.read",
  "exp": 1794445200,
  "act": { "sub": "agent:scheduling-assistant" }
}

Five fields answer the question in this article's title. sub says whose authority this is. act says who is using it. aud and scope say where and for what, and exp says until when. The calendar API can now apply a rule to the pair: Meera may delete events, but the scheduling agent acting for Meera may only read them. The audit log records both names.

Where this is still unfinished

It would be dishonest to present this as solved. Several separate Internet-Drafts on agent authorisation were circulating at the IETF in 2026, and none is a standard yet.

Scopes are also blunt. Auth0 points out that OAuth scopes can't easily express something like "contact details for the accounts I'm working on, but not the legal hold queue". Rules that fine need a policy check on every request, on top of the token.

And none of this helps if a second, broader credential is lying in a file the agent can read. That was the entire PocketOS failure.

An "Are you sure?" box is not authorisation

Many agent tools show a confirmation prompt before a risky step. That is useful, but it is weaker than it looks, for two reasons.

The prompt is drawn by the same software it is supposed to restrain. The IETF draft is blunt about this. A confirmation inside the agent's own interface does not count as authorisation unless it is tied to a grant from the authorisation server. The stronger pattern sends the approval request out of band, to the user's phone for example, with the details of the exact action attached. The draft admits that approvals in the middle of a running task still need more standards work.

The second reason is that words are not controls. The Replit user had told the agent not to make changes without permission. PocketOS had rules written into the agent's instructions. Telling an agent to stay out of production is a request. Removing its write access to production is a control, and only one of those survives a bad guess.

There is a human limit as well. Ask someone to approve every file read and by the afternoon they are approving everything. MCP's guidance lists users abandoning consent dialogs that ask for too much as a risk in its own right. Approval works when it is rare. Keep it for actions you can't take back: deleting data, moving money, sending something outside the company, changing who has access.

Seven questions before you hand an agent access

You don't need an identity platform to get most of the benefit. You need honest answers to these.

  1. Does the agent have its own identity, or is it borrowing mine or a shared one?
  2. If I read the audit log six months from now, will it show the agent, the person it acted for, and the action?
  3. What is the worst single call this credential can make? Find out before the agent does.
  4. When does this access end if I do nothing at all?
  5. Can I revoke it in one place, today, without breaking unrelated things?
  6. Which actions need a human yes, and is that yes enforced by the system or only by the prompt?
  7. What other credentials can the agent read from disk or from environment variables?

The last question is the one PocketOS missed, and it is the easiest to miss. An agent with shell access can read every secret in the working directory, whether or not you meant to hand it over. For a solo developer or a small team, the practical version is short. Give the agent a per-project token instead of an account-wide one. Point it at a read-only database user unless the task needs writes. Keep production secrets out of the folder it works in. Store backups somewhere the same credential can't reach.

What is the difference between authentication and authorisation for an AI agent?

Authentication proves which agent is calling. Authorisation decides what that agent may do. An agent can be perfectly authenticated and still hold far more access than its task needs.

Should an AI agent log in as me?

Preferably not. If the agent uses your login, every system treats its actions as yours and the logs can't tell the two of you apart. A delegated token that names both you and the agent keeps the record straight and lets you limit what the agent can do.

What does "on behalf of" mean in OAuth?

It describes a token that records two parties: the user whose authority is being used and the actor using it. RFC 8693 defines the token exchange that produces these tokens and the act claim that names the actor.

Does MCP take care of authorisation for me?

Partly. The MCP specification defines how a client gets an OAuth token for a remote server, ties that token to that one server and bans passing it on. It does not choose your scopes, and it can't stop a local agent from reading a broader key off your disk.

items.title: TikTok Shop Is Changing the Relationship Between Brands and Content Creators
items.author: Sanya Kapoor
items.content:
Image:-By Aidan Castillo, VP of Client Success at MediaLabs

The traditional consensus around influencer marketing primarily treated it as a means of generating awareness. Pay creators to introduce products to their audiences, hoping that attention eventually translates into sales.

Influencer marketing is now becoming a bottom-of-funnel channel, and TikTok Shop is substantially driving that evolution.

By integrating commerce directly into the content experience, the platform has made it possible for creators to influence purchasing decisions and facilitate transactions without directing consumers to external websites.

For brands, the implications extend well beyond another digital sales channel.

In my role as VP of Client Success at MediaLabs, I work with consumer brands developing their TikTok Shop strategies and the creators responsible for executing them.

One of the most significant changes I've observed is the growing importance of creators who aren't necessarily traditional influencers.

Historically, a creator's commercial value was closely tied to the size of their audience. Brands paid premiums for reach, even when the relationship between impressions and actual purchases was difficult to measure.

The idea of genuinely social commerce introduces a different set of considerations.

A creator with a relatively modest following can produce a video that directly generates substantial sales. Conversely, an established influencer with millions of followers isn't necessarily as readily equipped to sell a singular product directly.

The distinction matters because content performance and commercial performance are not interchangeable.

This changes how brands approach creator partnerships.

Rather than concentrating their budgets on a handful of expensive sponsorships, companies can work with larger networks of creators, test different approaches and identify which content consistently generates purchases.

At MediaLabs, our network includes more than 3,000 creators producing content for consumer brands.

During the first quarter of 2026, creators across our network generated approximately $19.35 million in gross merchandise value for participating brands. We also launched 29 creator retainer campaigns during that period.

These figures illustrate the scale at which creator-led commerce can operate, but they also point to an important operational challenge.

Managing a few influencer relationships is relatively straightforward. Coordinating hundreds of creators, maintaining content quality, evaluating performance and ensuring brands have consistent support requires considerably more infrastructure.

Training, creator selection, campaign management and ongoing communication become as important as the content itself.

There's also a meaningful change taking place on the creator side.

TikTok Shop has created opportunities for individuals to generate income through product recommendations without first establishing themselves as recognizable internet personalities.

That doesn't mean earning a sustainable income is easy. Competition is substantial, content performance varies, and creators must continually adapt to changing consumer preferences.

But the commercial opportunity is no longer reserved exclusively for people with enormous audiences.

As social commerce develops, I expect brands to place greater emphasis on measurable sales performance, repeatable creator partnerships and the systems required to manage them.

The companies that understand this distinction will be better positioned to evaluate TikTok Shop as a serious component of their broader e-commerce operations, rather than simply another outlet for influencer marketing.

items.title: How Context Graphs Speed Up Incident Response and Root Cause Analysis
items.author: PlayerZero
items.content:
A context graph links telemetry, deployments, code changes and support tickets into one connected model, so incident responders can trace what caused a production issue without jumping between tools.

Modern engineering teams already have the data they need to resolve incidents faster, reduce downtime, and ship with more confidence. The problem is that this data's fragmented across too many systems, making it difficult to understand how production issues actually unfold. When something breaks in production, engineers still waste valuable time jumping between observability tools, deployment history, support tickets, analytics platforms, and pull requests just to answer a simple question: What actually caused this issue?

That manual reconstruction slows incident response, pulls senior engineers away from roadmap work, and increases the operational cost of every release.

Context graphs solve this by connecting production signals into a shared reasoning layer that goes beyond code as the sole debugging surface. They connect telemetry, user impact, infrastructure events, and code changes into a unified system for understanding not just what happened, but why.

This guide explains why production understanding breaks down in modern systems and walks through three practical strategies for building a context graph that preserves operational context with every incident, instead of rebuilding it from scratch.

Why production understanding breaks down in modern systems

Modern engineering teams have invested heavily in specialized systems: observability platforms for infrastructure visibility, analytics tools for product insights, ticketing systems for customer operations, and CI/CD platforms for release orchestration.

The problem is that these tools were never designed to preserve causality across the full production lifecycle. Each system captures a partial view of reality, but none preserves the relationships between them.

Telemetry sees system behavior, not customer impact

Telemetry platforms are excellent at exposing runtime behavior: latency spikes, infrastructure anomalies, failing traces, and degraded dependencies.

But telemetry alone rarely explains:

  • Which users were affected
  • Whether support is already seeing escalations
  • Whether the issue traces back to a recent deployment

A spike in API latency may appear in Datadog within seconds, but engineers still need to determine whether it’s breaking checkout or only affecting an internal admin tool, whether the issue is isolated to one customer segment or spreading across the platform, and whether it maps back to the latest release.

As systems scale, a single runtime anomaly can propagate across dozens of services before teams understand the downstream customer impact.

Analytics sees behavior, not system dynamics

Analytics tools reveal what users are doing inside the product. Teams can quickly identify broken onboarding flows, declining engagement, and abnormal session behavior.

But analytics platforms typically lack:

  • Infrastructure dependencies

A product team may notice users abandoning a workflow after a deployment, but analytics alone cannot explain whether the issue came from backend latency, a failing dependency, a frontend rendering issue, or a configuration change introduced during release.

That disconnect creates friction across engineering, support, and product teams because each group sees a different version of the problem, but no system preserves the shared context that connects them.

Ticketing systems surface how issues appear to customers and stakeholders. Support and operations teams see failing workflows, frustrated users, and escalations tied to specific accounts and SLAs.

But most ticketing platforms fail to preserve the reasoning behind resolution. Once an incident closes, critical investigation context often disappears:

  • Which telemetry signals mattered
  • Which hypotheses engineers ruled out
  • Which runtime conditions shaped the issue
  • Which deployment triggered the regression
  • Why a remediation path succeeded

The result is a reconstruction tax across engineering organizations. Every major incident forces teams to manually reconnect dashboards, traces, session replay, deployment history, PRs, and institutional knowledge before they can begin fixing the problem itself.

Context graphs create a shared reasoning layer across production systems

Telemetry already knows when services fail and where latency spikes. Analytics knows which workflows users abandon. Ticketing systems know which customers are affected and how severe the escalations become.

The missing piece is how those signals relate across deployments, runtime conditions, user impact, and the decisions engineers made during resolution.

Context graphs solve this by acting as a connective reasoning layer across production systems.

Instead of treating telemetry, analytics, tickets, runtime behavior, and code as isolated datasets, a context graph connects them into a continuously evolving retrieval system that preserves how incidents, customer impact, and engineering decisions relate to one another over time.

That changes how engineering teams investigate issues in practice. Instead of manually stitching together dashboards, traces, tickets, and deployment history, teams can:

  • Trace anomalies back to the deployments that introduced them
  • Connect customer escalations to affected workflows and sessions
  • Identify which execution paths repeatedly appear across incidents

At PlayerZero, this retrieval layer forms the foundation of an engineering world model—accumulated operational context that compounds with every incident, deployment, and investigation.

Three strategies for building a context graph that scales

A context graph scales when it is built around the relationships engineers rely on most during debugging, release validation, and incident response.

The three strategies below break down how to build that layer in practice, from connecting production signals to using accumulated operational context before changes reach production.

Strategy 1: Build a retrieval layer anchored to stable execution paths

From an engineering perspective, building a context graph starts with a retrieval decision: what should be indexed ahead of time, what should be resolved dynamically at query time, and which systems are stable enough to serve as long-term reference points.

A useful context graph does not attempt to index every production signal equally. Instead, it prioritizes the execution paths engineers repeatedly traverse during debugging, incident response, release validation, and root-cause analysis.

In practice, that means connecting source code, PR history, telemetry traces, deployment metadata, support escalations, session replay data, and production events into a shared operational index. This also means precomputing indexes where schemas are stable and query volume is high—like code and PR history—and resolving more volatile, high‑cardinality signals, like telemetry parameters, at query time, rather than trying to index every possible relationship up front.

For most organizations, code becomes the natural anchor layer because it changes more slowly than runtime infrastructure and remains structurally consistent across investigations. Telemetry behaves differently: schemas evolve rapidly, infrastructure states shift continuously, and relationships across services become too large and short-lived to fully precompute.

That tradeoff is what makes code the most effective operational anchor. Instead of attempting to materialize every possible relationship across production systems, effective context graphs prioritize the operational pathways engineers revisit most often during real investigations.

How to implement a stable retrieval layer

  • Index source code and PR history so runtime signals can be traced back to execution paths
  • Map telemetry traces to the services and functions generating them
  • Link deployments to customer-facing regressions and support escalations
  • Connect user sessions to affected workflows and backend traces
  • Configure bidirectional traversal between incidents and implicated code paths
  • Prioritize indexing high-frequency workflows that engineers repeatedly investigate
  • Review recurring incident patterns quarterly to identify relationships worth preserving long-term

Key Data experienced this challenge as its platform expanded across increasingly complex customer workflows. Telemetry, runtime behavior, and execution paths lived in separate systems, forcing engineers into lengthy debugging cycles when customer-reported issues appeared. After PlayerZero anchored runtime behavior directly to code paths, teams could move from symptom to likely root cause in minutes instead of manually correlating evidence across multiple tools.

Strategy 2: Preserve operational trajectories as organizational memory

Most organizations preserve fixes but lose the investigation context behind them.

An incident may end with a rollback, patched dependency, or merged PR, but the reasoning that led to that resolution often disappears across Slack threads, ticket comments, deployment reviews, and fragmented debugging workflows.

A mature context graph solves this by preserving investigation trajectories instead of just final outcomes. It captures which telemetry engineers consulted, which execution paths were investigated, which runtime conditions mattered, and which remediation strategies succeeded.

Over time, those pathways become reusable operational memory. Instead of relying solely on institutional knowledge or senior engineer experience, teams can retrieve how similar incidents behaved historically, which remediation paths succeeded under specific runtime conditions, and which execution paths repeatedly introduced fragility.

The context graph learns which relationships matter most by observing how engineers actually traverse incidents, code paths, tickets, and telemetry during real investigations, and then prioritizing those pathways for deeper indexing.

Importantly, this does not require perfect documentation. Even partial preservation of investigation pathways creates compounding operational clarity.

How to preserve investigation trajectories

  • Attach telemetry traces and deployment metadata directly to incident tickets
  • Link remediation PRs back to the runtime conditions that triggered the issue
  • Preserve session replay data alongside escalation history during investigations
  • Add short investigation summaries before closing major incidents
  • Tag recurring failure pathways across services and releases
  • Create shared conventions for documenting remediation reasoning during incident response
  • Review recurring incidents monthly to identify patterns worth preserving permanently

Cayuse used PlayerZero to unify repositories, observability systems, support workflows, and telemetry into a connected operational layer that preserved investigation context across teams. With investigation history accessible in a shared system, engineers and support staff could resolve issues faster without repeatedly escalating problems to senior engineers for manual reconstruction.

Strategy 3: Use accumulated operational context to simulate failures before deployment

As context graphs accumulate operational history, engineering teams can begin using that context to evaluate how proposed changes might behave before they reach production.

Traditional testing validates expected functionality, predefined edge cases, and manually designed workflows. But many modern failures emerge from cross-service interactions, dependency behavior, infrastructure drift, deployment timing, and runtime conditions that engineers did not explicitly anticipate during development.

Context graphs add a different validation layer: accumulated production history. Instead of testing changes only against what engineers expected to happen, teams can evaluate them against prior incidents, historical runtime conditions, dependency relationships, deployment patterns, and previously observed failure pathways.

That changes release validation from static testing into historical reasoning. Every resolved incident becomes a reusable production scenario that informs future deployments.

As operational history compounds, the context graph gradually evolves into an engineering world model that represents how systems behave, how failures spread, and how runtime conditions influence reliability outcomes over time.

For engineering leaders, the long-term value is faster releases, fewer regressions, and more engineering capacity redirected from reactive debugging toward roadmap work.

How to use operational history for pre-deployment validation

Engineering teams should start simulation workflows in systems where incident history is already dense, regressions recur frequently, and release risk is consistently high.

  • Reuse resolved incidents as regression scenarios during PR validation
  • Run simulations against recent deployment patterns and runtime dependencies before merging changes
  • Validate changes against historically fragile execution paths and workflows
  • Compare simulation outcomes against post-release defect escape rates
  • Incorporate session replay and runtime traces into release validation workflows
  • Prioritize simulations around services with recurring escalation patterns
  • Expand simulation coverage incrementally as operational history accumulates

Cyrano Video used PlayerZero’s accumulated production context to assign risk levels to upcoming releases and identify issues tied to customer-facing workflows earlier in the validation process. That operational visibility helped teams prioritize remediation faster, improve release readiness, and reduce engineering effort spent on debugging after deployment.

The future of engineering velocity depends on persistent production understanding

The engineering teams that move fastest are not the ones with the most dashboards. They are the ones that preserve operational understanding across incidents, deployments, and production changes instead of reconstructing context from scratch every time something breaks.

As software systems become more distributed, AI-generated, and release-heavy, persistent production understanding becomes critical. The first step is to unify your core production signals, anchor them to code, and capture what you learned from each resolved incident.

PlayerZero builds and maintains that operational layer automatically, helping engineering organizations reduce repeated debugging work, improve release reliability, and ship more confidently at scale. items.title: AI Tool Adoption for Engineering Teams Isn't Enough
items.author: PlayerZero
items.content:
Adopting AI tools isn't an AI strategy: engineering teams see lasting gains only when their tools share context and AI activity ties back to business outcomes.

AI adoption is moving faster than most organizations' ability to define what success actually looks like. The industry is pulling in multiple directions at once: some leaders see AI as a productivity breakthrough, others see it as a threat to jobs, and many organizations are struggling to explain how AI activity translates into measurable business outcomes.

Inside engineering, that confusion is sharper. Most teams now have AI tools across the software delivery lifecycle: copilots for developers, QA automation, AI-assisted triage and support tools. But few organizations have defined what all of that AI activity is supposed to compound into.

The result is an AI tool strategy, not an AI strategy for engineering teams.

An AI strategy is not about maximizing usage across every function. It builds a shared picture of how software behaves in production, so engineering, QA, product, support, SRE, and leadership can reason from the same operational reality.

The cultural signals behind the AI strategy gap

That gap between tool adoption and real strategy is visible across industries, not just engineering organizations.

When former Google CEO Eric Schmidt was booed by graduates for mentioning AI during a commencement speech, the reaction revealed something more specific than job-displacement anxiety. It reflected growing skepticism toward productivity narratives that treat expertise as the thing AI is supposed to replace. That assumption is a design choice baked into how most engineering AI strategies are built.

Uber offers a different version of the same tension. In December 2025, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi framed AI as making engineers “superhumans.” By May 2026, the company was slowing hiring to fund AI investments, even as its COO acknowledged that the link between AI usage and measurable product outcomes remained unclear.

The issue was not simply that ROI measurement lagged adoption. The deeper problem was that the narrative about what AI would do arrived before organizations defined what it was supposed to improve. AI tools got deployed quickly, while the harder strategic questions about production outcomes and operational learning remained undefined.

At the same time, researchers like David Autor are pointing toward a more important distinction. The real question is not whether AI replaces human work. It is whether organizations use AI to make expert judgment more widely available or push humans further to the edges of decision-making.

That is the same strategic choice engineering organizations are now making, whether intentionally or not. Every AI workflow either helps distribute production judgment more broadly across the organization or concentrates operational expertise further inside the same small group of experienced engineers.

China’s approach to automation offers another institutional signal. Its AI strategy reflects an explicit decision to use automation to expand industrial capability and workforce productivity rather than treat automation primarily as a headcount reduction mechanism. What makes that approach instructive is not simply the scale of automation itself, but the sequencing behind it. Strategic intent came first. China defined what automation was supposed to accomplish before deploying it broadly.

Most engineering organizations are doing the reverse: adopting AI tools quickly and constructing the operational rationale afterward.

These signals are not contradictions. They are evidence of the same underlying gap: adoption is not strategy. Organizations that get this wrong treat expertise as the cost AI should remove. Organizations that get it right decide up front how AI should preserve, distribute, and extend production judgment across the business. That is the strategic question engineering leaders are now being forced to answer.

AI adoption is not the same as an AI strategy

When the first wave of AI tools entered engineering workflows, productivity gains were easy to understand. Code generation tools accelerated implementation. QA automation reduced manual work. Support triage tools helped teams process customer issues faster. SRE and observability assistants surfaced signals from noisy production systems more quickly. Product teams gained faster visibility into how features behaved in production and which changes drove customer impact.

For CTOs and engineering leaders, these tools appeared to solve an urgent business problem: improve software engineering productivity without scaling headcount at the same pace.

But most of these engineering productivity tools focused on accelerating pre-production workflows such as coding, testing, PR review, and ticket routing. Few organizations defined how AI should participate once software reached production or how those workflows should improve the organization’s ability to learn from incidents, regressions, and operational failures over time.

Developers optimized implementation. QA optimized test planning. Support optimized ticket intake. SRE optimized signal detection. But the operational knowledge generated by those workflows remained fragmented across teams and systems. As a result, every function became faster inside its own lane without improving how the organization understood production as a whole.

That is the difference between tool adoption and strategy. Tool adoption answers which AI tools the organization is using. Strategy answers what new organizational capabilities those tools are building.

Speed without shared context compounds operational complexity

The cost of an incomplete AI strategy becomes visible when every function accelerates in isolation, but the system remains just as hard to operate. For engineering teams, the real strategic test is whether every release, defect, escalation, and fix helps the organization better understand how its software behaves in production.

PR velocity improves, but MTTR does not fall proportionally. Support teams process more customer-facing tickets, but escalations still reach senior engineers. QA teams generate more test coverage, but production edge cases still escape. SRE tools surface more signals, but teams still spend hours reconstructing what changed, who owned it, and why customers were affected.

The problem is that local acceleration does not automatically reduce coordination cost. Teams end up adding more releases, alerts, AI-assisted changes, and operational signals into systems that are still just as difficult to understand when something breaks.

The hard work remains bottlenecked around reconstructing context, tracing causality, and relying on the same experienced engineers to connect fragmented information across the stack. This is the same failure pattern: adoption first, operational model second.

The metrics that define a durable AI strategy

A production-focused AI strategy for engineering teams is defined by improvements in operational outcomes, not just activity metrics like tool adoption, prompt volume, token consumption, and PR generation.

Mature teams treat tokens and agentic loops as units of work that represent specific outcomes rather than raw usage or increased code throughput. They are effectively buying work, not tries. AI ROI becomes legible when AI-assisted activity is tied to completed units of work and measurable improvements in MTTR, defect escape, incident volume, and senior engineering load.

The signal that an AI strategy is improving system quality shows up in production metrics:

  • Fewer customer-facing defects reaching production
  • Fewer unnecessary support escalations to engineering
  • Faster resolution of internal engineering issues
  • Less senior engineering time spent reconstructing context
  • Fewer repeated regressions from known failure modes

These outcomes reveal whether AI is reducing dependence on senior engineers or deepening it. Organizations that continue struggling with these outcomes often share the same underlying problem: their AI strategy stops at the point where code reaches production.

Why code generation alone can’t be your AI strategy

Code generation tools can accelerate implementation, but they do not address who carries production judgment once software reaches production.

AI coding tools are strongest before code reaches production: generating boilerplate, summarizing unfamiliar files, accelerating pull requests, and helping developers move through routine implementation work faster. But once an issue reaches production, the work stops being primarily a coding problem and becomes a context problem.

Production systems behave under conditions no isolated coding session can fully see, including customer-specific configurations, runtime dependencies, deployment timing, historical regressions, and operational signals spread across multiple systems.

Teams have to understand what the customer experienced, which code path was involved, what changed recently, whether the issue has happened before, and whether a fix creates risk somewhere else in the system. That investigation usually spans multiple tools and multiple teams, which means the engineers who already carry production judgment become an even greater bottleneck as AI-assisted development accelerates.

More AI-assisted changes flowing into production create more surface area for operational failures, but the judgment required to diagnose, contextualize, and resolve those failures still lives with the same small group of experienced engineers.

That is the hidden cost of adoption without strategy: faster implementation without a corresponding system for making operational expertise more reusable across the organization.

The missing piece is not another point solution. It is shared production intelligence.

Shared production intelligence is the missing piece

Shared production intelligence is a durable, shared picture of how software behaves in production, connecting code, tickets, telemetry, user sessions, deploys, dependencies, and resolution history into one operational layer that humans and AI agents can both reason from. Instead of every team working from its own incomplete slice of the system, engineering, QA, support, SRE, and leadership operate from that shared picture of production reality.

Without this layer, every function accelerates independently while the same coordination bottlenecks remain in place. Support surfaces more customer issues, QA generates more test coverage, and engineering ships changes faster, but senior engineers still carry the burden of reconstructing context whenever something breaks.

With shared production intelligence, those disconnected views begin to connect. A support ticket can be tied to a code path. A telemetry signal can be tied to a deploy. A regression can be tied to a prior fix. A customer-facing issue can be understood alongside affected users, historical incidents, and the system behavior behind it. MTTR and defect escape drop as operational knowledge from prior incidents, regressions, and fixes becomes broadly reusable across the organization.

This is where the AI strategy shifts from individual productivity to organizational intelligence. It is also the shift from single-player AI to multiplayer AI: away from isolated tools that accelerate individual workflows and toward a shared production model every function can use. Shared production intelligence gives those teams a common operational map.

How PlayerZero operationalizes shared production intelligence

Shared production intelligence does not make expert judgment irrelevant. It makes that judgment more durable and accessible by preserving the operational context that usually lives in Slack threads, incident memories, and the heads of senior engineers.

PlayerZero’s engineering world model is the architecture for this shared production intelligence. As investigations, fixes, escalations, and resolutions feed back into the model, production judgment becomes something the broader organization can reuse.

An SRE investigating a latency spike can move from telemetry to affected user sessions, recent code changes, and known regressions in a single view, reducing the time to resolution without pulling in the same handful of engineers to reconstruct context manually.

That is what enables AI-assisted work to compound into organizational intelligence instead of remaining isolated inside individual workflows.

AI tools attached to isolated workflows can accelerate local productivity while leaving the same coordination burden in place whenever something breaks. When AI-assisted workflows feed a shared production model instead, every incident, escalation, and resolution helps make production judgment more durable, reusable, and accessible across the organization.

That is where AI investment starts to compound: not through more tools attached to isolated functions, but through a shared understanding of how software behaves in production. The next phase of AI maturity is shared operational context across the full software lifecycle.

Most engineering leaders running AI tools right now are seeing this pattern. The question is not whether they bet on the wrong tools—it is what comes after AI code generation tools.

items.title: Medical AI Has a Trust Problem That Better Technology Alone Can't Fix
items.author: Sanford Diday
items.content:
Approval is not proof: AI changed how fast claims arrive, not what it takes to know they are true.

Three months ago, I argued that artificial intelligence had changed the volume, speed, and polish of information moving through the world without changing the standard that makes any individual claim reliable. The responsibility for separating one from the other, I argued, has never belonged to a piece of technology. It belongs to whoever decides what to believe, and to whoever approves what other people may use. Nothing in the three months since has required a correction. If anything, confirmation arrived from an unexpected direction: a government audit of the tools doctors use to write down what their patients tell them.

The Case Nobody Was Watching For

On May 12, 2026, Ontario’s Auditor General, Shelley Spence, released a special report on the government’s use of artificial intelligence. One section examined Ontario’s AI Scribe. Ontario promoted AI scribes to physicians in 2024, and the vendor-of-record approvals followed in April 2025 (“Ontario AG Finds Flaws in AI Scribes”; Hauen; Vescera and Giancola). The Auditor General’s own announcement described “limited use of security assessment reports, bias testing and live demonstrations of the AI Scribe systems for health care” among already-approved vendors (Office of the Auditor General of Ontario, “Ontario Auditor General Releases”). Evaluators tested twenty approved vendors against two simulated doctor-patient conversations each, then checked the notes against what was actually said. The results were not close. Nine of the twenty systems invented clinical details never discussed, including therapy referrals and blood tests no one had ordered. Twelve recorded a different medication than the one the doctor actually prescribed. Seventeen missed a key detail about the patient’s mental health in at least one of the two tests (“AI Transcriber for Use by Ontario Doctors ‘Hallucinated’”; Vigliarolo). Ontario approved five of the twenty vendors even though they had not submitted the risk and privacy assessments the process required (“Ontario AG Finds Flaws in AI Scribes”). Eleven of the twenty submitted no third-party audit reports at all (“Ontario AG Finds Flaws in AI Scribes”). The report put it bluntly: “Inaccuracies in medical notes generated by AI scribe systems could potentially result in inadequate or harmful treatment plans that may potentially impact patient health outcomes” (Office of the Auditor General of Ontario, Use of Artificial Intelligence, sec. 4.3).

The scoring method helps explain why Ontario approved inaccurate vendors. Of 530 points in the bidding criteria, a vendor’s domestic presence in Ontario carried a maximum of 159, about thirty percent. The accuracy of a vendor’s medical notes carried a maximum of 20, about four percent (Office of the Auditor General of Ontario, Use of Artificial Intelligence, app. 2, pp. 46–47). Bidders could have scored zero on system security, bias controls, and note accuracy and still met the minimum score for approval (Hauen). A process weighting criteria this way risks more than approving an inaccurate vendor: it can let an inaccurate vendor outscore an accurate one on criteria unrelated to whether a transcript is true.

Where the System Still Depended on a Human

None of this is a story about careless technology. AI scribes exist to solve a real problem: physicians spending unpaid hours each week typing notes instead of treating patients. Spence called the tools problematic but said “AI is a tool that will improve efficiencies and delivering services [sic]” (D’Mello and Callan). Ontario’s Minister of Public and Business Service Delivery and Procurement, Stephen Crawford, made a fair point in response: physicians oversee every aspect of the product. The errors, he said, surfaced during a testing phase meant to catch them before deployment, not during an actual patient visit (“AI Transcriber for Use by Ontario Doctors ‘Hallucinated’”). The point is incomplete, though: finding errors during testing is not itself evidence of failure, because testing exists to expose weaknesses before they reach patients. Still, a test protects patients only when its findings meaningfully affect approval, remediation, or deployment. According to the Auditor General’s office, all twenty approved systems showed at least one inaccuracy at the procurement testing phase, and there was no evidence of additional testing or evaluation at the time of the audit (D’Mello and Callan). Ontario approved them anyway. Physician oversight is also thinner than the minister’s framing suggests: none of the approved systems required doctors to sign off on notes (Office of the Auditor General of Ontario, Use of Artificial Intelligence, sec. 4.3). The test worked. The approval process did not adequately act on what the test revealed.

A related weakness appeared elsewhere. The Investigative Journalism Foundation reported that ADGScribe, an approved vendor, had published testimonials from two physicians who appear to be nonexistent (Vescera and Giancola; Raza and Spithoff). That would be a fabricated source, one that reached physicians who had no reason to doubt it and could shape a purchasing decision through endorsements nobody made. In both cases, approval tells physicians that someone has already tested the source and found it truthful. The dangerous output was not only the inaccurate note or the invented endorsement. It was the institutional signal someone had already checked the system adequately. The physicians who choose one of these vendors trust a process strangers ran, on a product whose failure mode looks like a correctly written note, or a genuine endorsement, until someone checks what was actually said, or who actually said it.

In my earlier piece, I proposed a three-part test for claims like this: Source, Method, and Motive. Each asks a different question when I apply it to a system instead of a sentence. Source asks where a claim originated, not merely that something which sounds official vouches for it: an approved vendor is not the same claim as an accurate transcript, and a doctor’s testimonial is not the same claim as a doctor. Method asks whether the output rests on the underlying evidence: a system capable of producing fluent clinical prose can generate a note that reads coherently even when the recorded conversation does not support parts of it. Motive asks who benefits if readers accept the claim: a vendor benefits from passing procurement and from an unchecked testimonial, and a government has reason to want a burnout-easing program to succeed. Neither interest has anything to do with whether a specific note or endorsement is accurate.

Hearing Out the Other Side

Not everyone who has studied this audit agrees it describes the tools doctors use today. Will Falk, a Toronto-based consulting executive who tracks AI adoption in Canadian health care, argued that the audit evaluated an earlier generation of the vendors’ products, and that today’s scribes have since improved (“Ontario AG Finds Flaws in AI Scribes”). Falk cited figures indicating 28 percent of Canadian physicians use AI scribes and three-quarters of those physicians use them daily, which raises the stakes of judging whether the audited products still match what doctors use now (“Ontario AG Finds Flaws in AI Scribes”). Dr. Paul Forman, a family physician in Markham, Ontario, added a related point: these tools reduce burnout because they work well most of the time, and the honest standard was never perfection. “No matter how advanced a system is, no system can ever claim 100% accuracy or efficiency,” he said (“Ontario AG Finds Flaws in AI Scribes”). The ministry has likewise said about 5,000 physicians use AI scribes, with no known reports of patient harm (“AI Transcriber for Use by Ontario Doctors ‘Hallucinated’”). These objections limit what the audit can tell us about the present accuracy of individual products. They do not answer the audit’s central procurement finding: Ontario approved vendors through a process placing little weight on accuracy and accepting critical assurances without consistent independent verification.

The Part of the Story AI Did Not Create

None of this is new, a point worth making to anyone tempted to treat AI Scribe as a uniquely artificial-intelligence failure. Procurement processes have always worked as vouching mechanisms officials run on behalf of people who were not in the room for the testing. A pharmaceutical label, a safety certification, and a credit rating all perform a similar institutional function: they allow people who cannot independently reproduce an evaluation to rely on someone else’s verification. Two family physicians who reviewed the audit for Healthy Debate argued the AI Scribe rollout amounted to a test run for a larger project: a province-wide electronic medical record system that will carry far more patient data than any single transcript (Raza and Spithoff). What AI adds to this older procurement problem is not a new category of risk. It adds scale and fluency to an old one. A fabricated blood-test referral reads exactly like a real one, with none of the tells, misspellings, or implausible claims that once flagged a human transcription error for a second look. The claim sounds no different whether it is true or not.

What Three Months Confirmed

The audit required no new theory of how artificial intelligence works. It required Ontario’s Auditor General to do a job older than any government software: checking whether an approval process does what it promised. Spence did not conclude Ontario should abandon AI Scribe. Her ten recommendations aimed mostly at tightening security, privacy, and testing requirements. Supply Ontario agreed to review best practices and to require yearly external audits, but it disagreed with raising the weight on security and privacy (Hauen). That is responsible verification at work: not a referendum on the technology, but an ordinary check on a process meant to catch the problem.

The Ontario audit demonstrated an old rule of institutional trust: approval is not proof, fluency is not accuracy, and a process protects the public only when someone acts on what the process discovers. AI made unsupported claims easier to produce and harder to recognize. It did not change the questions we must ask to assess them. Those remained human questions:

  1. What is the source of this claim?
  2. Who benefits if I accept it without checking?

Some tricks are surprisingly easy to pull off. A few commands, and your laptop starts looking like something out of a sci-fi movie.

Here are five fun tricks you can try on macOS, Windows, or Linux. And don't worry, you don't need to be a programmer to follow along.

1. Kill a Frozen App From Terminal

The next time a program freezes, there’s a much cooler solution than desperately clicking around and tearing your hair out. You can terminate the frozen app directly from the terminal—which, let’s be real, feels like you’re in charge.

2. Use a Video as Your Screensaver

Most of us have boring screensavers.

But imagine walking away from your computer and watching a spaceship dashboard, a cyberpunk city, or your own hacker screen appear.

This trick swaps one of Apple’s downloaded screensaver videos for a video saved on your computer.

Select that screensaver again in Settings. The option still looks like Apple’s original, but it now plays your video.

One catch: this is an unofficial workaround from the Sonoma era. Later macOS updates may block it or change where the files are stored, and playback can be unreliable.

Windows doesn't natively offer a general-purpose option for setting an MP4 file as a screensaver.

After installing a trusted utility, configure your video file and open the Windows screensaver settings.

Select the installed screensaver and set the idle timeout.

You can also use animated wallpaper software for a similar effect, although an animated wallpaper isn't technically a screensaver.

Linux offers more flexibility, although the setup depends on your desktop environment and whether you're using X11 or Wayland.

On X11, a tool such as can be combined with a video player to create a looping video background.

This is a video wallpaper rather than a true idle-triggered screensaver. You would need additional idle detection and lock-screen integration to reproduce the full screensaver behavior.
